records.name: Gyeonggi
records.summary:
The model student human-rights ordinance covering discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity was first enacted in 2010 by a progressive superintendent of education for Gyeonggi Province; Seoul's office adopted it in 2012 and it spread to other regional offices before the 2024–26 repeal wave.

When Seoul's metropolitan council — pushed by a campaign begun by religious and parents' coalitions in August 2022 — abolished the capital's ordinance on 26 April 2024, Gyeonggi stood among only six regional education offices still enforcing comparable ordinances, and a Gyeonggi-based teacher warned that wholesale abolition 'will bring a regression to human rights in the education sector'. The province's standing is thus origin-and-retention of student protections rather than any enforcement measure aimed at visitors.

records.summary:
Arica y Parinacota is grouped with Tarapacá in the dossier under the heading "the northern courts' non-recognition of trans women as women," reflecting the shared judicial geography of northern Chile. However, the specific Iquique Court of Appeals annulment was delivered in Tarapacá, and Arica's own data contribution is limited to a 0.84 % share of national cases (2024). No trans-specific incident, court ruling, or enforcement failure originating in Arica was identified. The deviation below national rests on the shared northern judicial-climate framing and the broader pattern — reported for both the 2024 and 2025 Movilh annual surveys — that homo/transphobia cases rose in most regions outside the metropolitan core.

Against the national 0.72, this is a −0.03 deviation, the smallest in the scored set. Compared with Tarapacá (0.64), Arica is 0.05 higher because it lacks the concrete femicide-annulment ruling; the northern-court context applies but is not evidenced with a named local finding. Compared with Ñuble (0.67), Arica is 0.02 higher: Ñuble's +300 % surge is a more specific and dramatic statistical signal than Arica's sub-percent case share.

records.name: Bayern
records.summary:
Since 1 April 2024, gender-inclusive German has been prohibited in schools, universities and all state administration in Bavaria, implementing the Söder government declaration of December 2023 through a cabinet decision amending the language rules of public authorities. Coverage notes critics dismissing the measure as symbol politics while recording its practical reach across every public counter, registry office and classroom a visitor might deal with.

Bavaria is also a partner — with Sachsen, Thüringen and Sachsen-Anhalt — in a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act (SBGG) on legal gender change: an organised state-level attempt to make the nationwide self-ID law stricter, which critics see as restricting how trans and intersex people use the right.
